Measuring pipeline latency without instrumenting every job

Published 28 March 2026 by Priya Raman.

Pipeline latency is the time between a source system recording a fact and that fact becoming queryable in the warehouse. Most teams try to measure pipeline latency by adding timing code to every scheduled job, which is accurate and almost never finished, because there is always one more job nobody instrumented.

Measure from warehouse metadata instead

Every major warehouse already records when each table was last written. Snowflake exposes this in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES as LAST_ALTERED, BigQuery in __TABLES__ as last_modified_time, and Postgres through pg_stat_user_tables. Reading those columns on a schedule gives a latency figure for every table in the warehouse without touching a single job definition.

What the metadata approach misses

Warehouse metadata records when a table was written, not whether the write was correct. A job that runs on time and loads zero rows looks healthy by this measure. Pair the freshness signal with a row-count delta so an empty load is caught as well as a late one.

How much this catches in practice

Across the 2025 Northwind Analytics customer cohort, 71 percent of stale-table incidents were detectable from warehouse metadata alone, and median time to detection fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes. The remaining 29 percent required a row-count or schema check, which is why we ship both.

Further reading

The freshness-versus-correctness distinction is set out well in the data quality literature, and the warehouse metadata columns are documented in each vendor’s own reference.
